text: “SUNNING” EXPLOIT.

label: text
text: lin' It was on "their anxiety to distinguish these lights that advantage was taken by the 2nd Officer and Captain to make the first blow for the reassertion of control by the officers.

label: paragraph_title
text: Tables "Turned."

label: paragraph_title
text: Officers Overpower Pirates on Bridge.

label: text
text: Shortly before midnight, eight hours after the pirates had assumed control, the 2nd Officer suddenly pointed to distant lights and called to the pirates covering him with their revolvers. "There are the lights of Chilang Point," Turning to look, the pirates were momentarily off their guard and the 2nd Officer seized the opportunity of hitting both on the head with a deep-sea sounding lend. The two officers, in possession of the revolvers of the two pirates in question, had a commanding position from the bridge.

label: text
text: Of the subsequent happenings—the defence of the bridge throughout the night against onslaughts by the pirates in the course of which eleven were shot dead; the unsuccessful ruse of the pirates to regain possession of the bridge by pushing the Chief Engineering in front of them; the joining of the Captain and 2nd Officer on the bridge by the Mate and other officers who were pulled up through a skylight from the room in which they have been locked when the pirates first gained control—of this, and much else, little other than the barest details are obtainable from the officers who participated.

label: text
text: In spite of the reticence of the officers to detail the parts which each played in this epic of the sea, the story already published bears tribute to their gallant conduct throughout a night whence danger threatened from almost every quarter. It might be added that communication between the officers on the bridge and those mentioned yesterday as having been locked in and guarded by pirates in the Mate's room was restored through the lulling of the suspicions of the pirates by the friendly attitude of the officers.

label: text
text: After the ship had been in the possession of the pirates for some six or seven hours and, knipwing the officers to be unarmed, the pirates allowed them to go to the saloon and it was here, that on the action being taken by the officers on the bridge, the officers below joined them by breaking a sky-light and being pulled above whilst the guards below hastened to find out what the shooting was about. The officers were preceded by the Russian lady passenger who was hoisted first on to the bridge.

label: paragraph_title
text: No Armistice.

label: paragraph_title
text: Pirates' Request Refused By Officers.

label: text
text: To the danger from lurking foes was added that of fire, the pirates lighting large quantities of waste under the bridge in the hope that the officers would be smoked out. The set of the wind was against the object, however, and the pirates themselves were in it inent danger from the flames which spread to the quarter where they had taken up their stand.

label: text
text: The officers on the bridge, strengthened by those who had joined them below through the searchlight, were in a strong position and, recognising the helplessness of their case, the pirates endeavoured to treat with the officers through Mr. Lapsley, the European passenger who is still unaccounted for—having, it is believed, been taken away by the pirates.

label: text
text: The pirates indicated their willingness to cease hostilities if the officers would give up their arms and combine in ences to get the flames under. The overtures were ignored and the pirates then left the ship, as already detailed. This was about 4 a.m.

label: text
text: It was subsequent to the departure of the two boat loads of pirates that the two officers and wireless operator left the ship in the remaining boat with the Russian lady passenger, the fire being at its worst at the time and the action being taken as a result of a consultation between the officers who deemed it the most advisable course. The boat was being threatened by the flames and the opportunity to place the lady passenger in safety might not have arisen again. It was also intended to place on board the Chinese lady passengers, but the half burned painter parted and the boat drifted away.

label: text
text: “Sheep” And “Goats.” The subsequent events consisted of the arrival on the scene in

label: text
text: the early hours of "Tuesday morning of the "Kalyo Maru," the first to wireless the report which was picked up by H.M.S. "Bluebell," the standing by of the "Kalying" and "Suiyang," the quelling of the flames and the boarding of the victimised vessel by an armed party from the "Bluebell" which "sorted out the sheep from the gouts" and put the suspected pirates into irons (they were met in some cases with resistance and had to use force).

label: text
text: In connection with the arrival of the “Kaiyo Muru” and other vessels which stood by, the officers of the “Sunning” report that prior to the arrival of the Japanese vessel, a ship loomed up about three miles away at a time when the ship was blazing and the officers still engaged in defending the bridge against the pirates. This was the hour before dawn. To their astonishment and bitter disappointment, the “mystery vessel,” after heaving to at the sight of the blazing “Sunning,” from which frantic signals of distress were made, proceeded on its course, leaving the stricken ship tossing and burning in the heavy seas.

label: text
text: The tug from Taikoo arrived on the scene at 9:20 p.m. on Tuesday night and within three quarters of an hour was able to hitch up securely and get under way. The tug averaged 7 knots an hour on her way to Hong Kong, a remarkable achievement considering the high seas running and the heavy burden.

label: text
text:
Five Thrown Overboard.
Among the Chinese crew, there were but minor casualties, a few having received superficial wounds in pluckily resisting the pirates. Five members of the compradore's staff are said to have been thrown overboard, this being due to their loyalty to the No. 1 compradore whom the pirates are reported to have been desirous of securing for the purpose of holding him to ransom.

label: text
text:
Compradore's Escape.
At the first sign of trouble, the compradore, having blackened his face with oil and coal dust, joined with the members of the crew and escaped observation. Enquiries by the pirates among the compradore staff and crew, and threats used towards the bo'sun failed toicit information as to his wherebouts and the pirates had to be satisfied with leaving the ship without having secured

label: text
text:
the ship without having secured
him.

label: text
text: One Annamite (third class) passenger is also stated to be missing. It is stated by other passengers that he was thrown overboard by the pirates for resisting search.

label: paragraph_title
text: Grim Relics

label: text
text: Charred Bones of Pirates on “Sunning.”

label: text
text: On the arrival of the “Sunning” off Taikoo and the boarding by officials, “grim relics of the fight and conflagration were still to be observed among the charred beams and woodwork, twisted bars and other remnants of what had been the bridge and amidship accommodation of the officers and passengers.

label: text
text: The height to which the flames rose when the fire was at its worst could be gauged by the funnel, marks of scorching and blackening extending half way up its length. Forward and aft there remained little signs of the conflagration, the fire merely having blackened and scorched the derricks lying across the hatches.

label: text
text: Lying on the remains of a sky-light was a heap of charred bones, all that was left of a pirate who had fallen when shot from the bridge and been unable to move when the flames reached the spot where he had fallen.

label: text
text: Yet another gruesome sight in the bunk of what had been a cabin was that of the charred remains of a pirate who, apparently having been wounded, had "dragged" himself to what he considered a place of safety—only to find himself trapped and unable to move when the fire broke out at the instance of his fellow conspirators.

label: text
text: On the "arrival aboard of the Police and other officials, several of the arrested men, stated to have participated in the combined attack of the pirates, were sent off under Police supervision, all being managed. Others, one of whom is thought to be mortally wounded and two bearing marks of severe head wounds, were taken off for medical attention. The corpses of the pirates who were shot dead were also taken away by launch.

label: text
text: Each of the remaining passengers was closely examined by Police officials before being allowed to leave the ship, statements being taken from each and some being detained pending a satisfactory explanation.

label: text
text: There remained but four of the officers aboard, when the "Sunning" anchored off Taikoo yesterday, these being the skipper. Capt.

label: text
text: J. Pringle, the Chief Officer, T. Beatty, the Second Engineer, W. Orr, and the wounded Chief Engineer, G. Cormack.

label: text
text: Mr. Cormack was taken ashore and removed by ambulance. Although wounded in the chest and thigh he was cheerful and able to converse freely.

label: paragraph_title
text: Loss By Fire.

label: paragraph_title
text:
Percena¹ Effets And Mall
Bags Burnt.

label: text
text: The other officers on board, apart from the marks their uniforms bore of their struggle with the flames, and their unshaven appearance, bore few signs of the terrific strain through which they had passed. The flames had not left a vestige of their equipment, papers and personal effects, or of those of the two European passengers. "We have nothing other than we stand up in," said one officer whose uniform had been so badly burned that he had discarded it for a sweater.

label: text
text: The 2nd Officer and Third Engineer, Messrs. J. W. Hurst and A. Duncan respectively, the only other European officers not already mentioned, were those "picked up by the Norwegian vessel which stood by and later conveyed them northwards, together with Mrs. A. Prokofiers. They were the officers who were lowered into the one remaining bout for the purpose of ensuring the safety of the lady passenger. The Norwegian vessel landed them at Swatow.

label: text
text: In addition to the personal effects lost, two mail bags were burned. These were despatched from Amoy for Hong Kong and Canton. The bulk of the mail carried was from Shanghai and this was untouched together with the cargo.

label: text
text:
Cargo and Engines: Untouched.
This was due to the fire being entirely confined to midships, the most remarkable thing striking the observer being the suddenness with which all traces of the fire ceased on either side. The cargo engine room and other parts of the ship were entirely unaffected. The "Sunning" could, in fact, have come to Hong Kong without tow had it not been for the fact that, having lost steam, she could not get it up again.

label: paragraph_title
text: TOLD TO WORLD.

label: text
text: Rugby's Wireless Version of "Sunning" Affair.

label: text
text: The following version of the "Sunning" piracy is interesting in that it is the "official" story, as given out to the world through the agency of the British Wireless Service.

label: text
text: It contains many inaccuracies, however. No. "hostages" were taken by the pirates, the officers and passenger picked up in a lifeboat having left the ship when the fire was at its height.

label: text
text:
The ship's engines were not dis-
abled by the pirates. The vessel
was merely unable to raise steam.
The message is as follows:—

label: text
text: A serious case of piracy has occurred on the British steamer "Sunning" a 2,555 tonnage belonging to the China Navigation Company, Chinese pirates, masquerading as passengers, having attempted to seize the vessel on her voyage from Shanghai to Hong Kong.

label: text
text: The ship's officers put up a determined resistance, one being wounded. The pirate, after setting fire to the ship, left in boats, taking with them Europeans, including two women as hostages. Reports state that the attack occurred early yesterday morning, the ship's engines and wireless being disabled.

label: text
text: A heavy sea was running. A Japanese vessel sighted the helpless and burning vessel and wirelessly lessed for assistance. The British destroyer "Bluebell" raced to the scene and, despite the extremely rough weather conditions,-board-ed the "Sunning" arrested several pirates still aboard and subdued the fire.

label: text
text: Other vessels also approached and leaving them to tow the "Sunning," the "Bluebell" began to search for pirates, discovering a boatload. Other British naval vessels and seaplanes joined in the search later finding an empty lifeboat. The Norwegian steamer "Rayensjell" picked up a boat containing three officers and one European woman.

label: paragraph_title
text: RIGID SEARCH.

label: text
text: Chinese opinion in Hong Kong is unanimous that rigid search is necessary at all ports of call on river and/or coastal boats bound for Hong Kong

label: text
text: At the same time, the local authorities are praised for their vigilance in having scared away

label: text
text: piratus gangs from Hong Kong so that they must ship at other places. Criticism of the alleged unwarranted rigour exercised by searchers on Hong Kong wharves has considerably moderated. Sympathy is expressed with the officers crew and passengers of the "Sunning" for their terrible ordeal, but they are thought lucky for not having had to abandon the ship in the confusion of the night when beset by flames as was the case with the "Tai On."

label: text
text: Chinese engaged in the shipping trade are still against suggestions to segregate native passengers while under way on account of possible dangers at sea and making too many innocent sufferer for the sins of the few.

label: text
text: The principal of a firm of Shanghai merchants in Hong Kong said: "It is impossible at present to expect our (the Chinese) Navy to perfect a system of patrols or convoys which foreign warships are put to considerable trouble in maintaining over even a small area.

label: text
text: "Every gang has been traced to Bias Bay except the outlaws on the West and East Rivers (of Kwangtung) who are also bandits and robbers and these are scattered over hills in the adjoining territory."

label: text
text:
Novel Chinese Solution.
"Bias Bay will provide the solution. A precedent exists, as extradition treaties are provided to help friendly nations in arresting prisoners. Therefore the only cure is for the Nationalist Government to provide the troops and to ask for the co-operation of foreign Navies in a campaign at Rias Bay.

label: text
text:
The object, however, should be solely the hunting down of the pirate gangs, and not the bombarding of the vicinity at random.
"After that the local military commanders could hold the elders and headmen of each community responsible for their respective clans not having any pirates, at home or abroad. Severe penalties for clansmen would have sufficient deterrent effect on the erring brethren, or the others would see to it that the offenders were delivered to justice."

label: text
text: "This practice was followed with conspicuous success in the latter years of the Manchu dynasty, when Kwangtung was free from robber bands."

label: text
text: A former compradore on a Jardine boat in North China said he very much doubted if the killing and arrest of part of one gang would serve as a lesson to others

label: text
text: His experience of pirates was that they did things on a very businesslike scale and took the expense (including purchase of passages, possible loss of their weapons) as being more important than the risk entailed.

label: text
text: JAPAN SENDING CRUISER.

label: paragraph_title
text: Tokyo, Nov. 17.

label: text
text: Owing to the request of Japanese business men at Canton the Navy Office has decided to employ a warship on permanent guard against Chinese pirates.

label: text
text: It is understood that the cruiser "Tsushima" is being despatched, but later the gunboat "Uji," which is undergoing repairs, will relieve her.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: WARSHIPS RETURN.

label: text
text: The nine pirates captured in one of the “Sunning’s” lifeboats by H.M.S. “Bluebell” were brought to Hong Kong and handed over to the Police officials.

label: text
text: H.M.S. "Vindictive" and H.M.S. "Despatch," which were sent to the scene on news of the piracy being received in Hong Kong on Tuesday, returned to port yesterday afternoon.

label: text
text: 'Planes from the "Hermes" have been keeping the vicinity of the piracy under observation but no further captures or the sighting of any further lifeboats are reported.

label: paragraph_title
text: MR. HO KOM-TONG.

label: text
text: STARTS AS RACE-PONY OWNER.

label: text
text: FIRST GRIFFIN ARRIVES

label: text
text: Yesterday the first China pony griffin arrived in Hong Kong from the North for Ho Kom-tong, the well-known Chinese resident and Corps Superintendent of St. John Ambulance. Brigade.

label: text
text: Mr. Ho intends to enter a string of new ponies in the 1927 Hong Kong Derby to be run next spring and he has also subscribed for a number of subscription griffins of the Hong Kong Jockey Club.

label: text
text: As a race-goer, Mr. Ho has already been very popular with the officials, owners, ockeys and even the humble manfo.

label: text
text: His advent in local racing circles—it being the first occasion on which Chinese will figure as owners—will be hailed with delight by his many friends.

label: paragraph_title
text: CANTON ADVANCE.

label: text
text: London, Nov.

label: text
text: In the House of Commons, to-day, in answer to questions, the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Sir Austen Chamberlain, said that the advance of the southern forces in Central China did not appear to have adversely affected the personal security of British residents or to have involved any serious danger to British property, though inevitably there had been some disturbance to British establishments in the army zone.

label: text
text:
The anti-British agitation in Szechuan had led to the destruction of some British property at Chungking, and it had been considered advisable for the women and children to leave that port.
Conditions in mid-China were still uncertain, and it would be premature to pass judgment.
Questioned as regards the "Sunning" incident, Sir Austen Chamberlain asked for notice of the question. He also requested notice of the question whether he could assure the House that there was a sufficient naval force at Hankow to ensure the safety of British residents there in case of need.—Reuter.

label: text
text:
In an article in the "Financial News" on the Chinese crisis, Mr. Hilton Young says, the establishment of the rule of Southern Nationalists throughout China, which recent events have made by no means improbable, would result in a vast area inhabited by nearly one fifth of the world's population erecting between itself and the rest of the world the same impenetrable barrier of suspicion, distrust and dislike at present isolating Russia, and thus the basis of credit would be destroyed and international trade would languish.
He says that recent events in Java show how infectious Moscow's propaganda is among an ignorant Oriental population, and opines that Britain's best policy is to approach the Canton Government, giving it some qualified form of recognition, and seek to guide it away from the path of repudiation, so ruinous to China herself.—Reu

label: text
text: The Foreign Office hitherto has not replied to the Belgian Legation concerning the proposal to submit the question of treaty abrogation to the Hague, but certain Chinese and foreign papers to-day state that preparations are being made for an anti-Belgian boycott if Belgium does so.—Reuter.

label: text
text: Senator Borah in the course of an address to Jewish women said the present turmoil in China furnished the acid test of the world peace programme.

label: text
text: Senator Borah's View's.

label: text
text: He opined the real trouble in China was nationalism coming into contact with imperialism. "Any nation which adopted a policy of forcible intervention, there will become the assassin of justice in the Orient."—Reuter's American Service.

label: paragraph_title
text: FURTHER PROGRESS.

label: paragraph_title
text: IMPERIAL CONFERENCE WORK

label: text
text: It now seems probable that the Imperial Conference will be brought to a close by the evening of Tuesday next.

label: text
text: Good progress has been made with the work before the committees of the Conference, and most of them will have completed their tasks of the end of the week.

label: text
text: Several of the committees' reports will be considered at tomorrow's plenary session, and these will include the report on production and exhibition within the Empire of films of Empire origin, which was approved by the economic committee to-day.—British Wireless Service.

label: text
text: He replied that no, decisions were taken or sought at the meeting. He had, however, taken the opportunity of assuring His Excellence of the British Government's desire to co-operate with the Egyptian Government, and he had received His Excellence's assurances that the Egyptian Government shared that desire. British Wireless Service
